prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
Inside the .git directory, Git is a key-value database in which every value is addressed by a hash of its own contents, and the objects directory holds the values while a handful of small text files hold the names that make them findable. When you run git add on a file, Git compresses the file's bytes with zlib, prepends a short header consisting of the word blob, a space, the byte length and a null byte, and computes a SHA-1 hash (or SHA-256 in repositories created with that option) over the header plus the contents. The resulting 40-character hex string becomes the object's identity, and the compressed data is written to .git/objects under a directory named for the first two characters of the hash and a file named for the remaining thirty-eight. This stored object is a blob, and it contains nothing except the file's contents: no filename, no permissions, no timestamp. Two files with identical text anywhere in your project, or in any commit in history, share a single blob, and a file you edit produces a brand new blob while the old one stays exactly where it was, since an object cannot change without its hash changing too.

Because blobs carry no names, something else has to say which blob is which file, and that is the job of the tree object. A tree represents one directory and is a sorted list of entries, each holding a mode, a name and the hash of the thing it points to, which is a blob for a file or another tree for a subdirectory. The mode distinguishes a regular file (100644) from an executable (100755), a symbolic link (120000), a subdirectory (040000) or a submodule pointer (160000), and Git records nothing finer than that, so the full permission bits you know from the filesystem never enter the repository. A tree for your project root might list a README blob, a src subtree and a package manifest blob, and the src tree in turn lists its own files, so that the hash of the root tree is effectively a fingerprint of the whole project at one instant: change one character in one deeply nested file and that file's blob hash changes, which changes the hash of its parent tree, which changes the hash of every tree above it up to the root. The same mechanism lets unchanged directories be reused untouched between snapshots, because an unchanged subtree has an unchanged hash and so is simply referenced again. Between your working directory and these trees sits the index, a binary file at .git/index listing the paths and blob hashes you have staged, and the tree objects for a new commit are built from it, which explains why staging and committing are separate steps.

A commit object is a small text record that points at one of these root trees and adds the history around it. It begins with a tree line naming the root tree's hash, followed by one parent line for each preceding commit (none for the very first commit, one for ordinary commits, two or more for merges), then an author line and a committer line each carrying a name, an email address, a Unix timestamp and a timezone offset, and finally a blank line and your commit message. Since the parent hash is part of the text being hashed, a commit's identity depends on its entire ancestry, which is why rewriting an old commit through a rebase or amend yields new hashes for that commit and every descendant, and why two people who share a hash are guaranteed to share identical history behind it. Notably, a commit stores no diff at all; the changes you see in git show or git log -p are computed on demand by comparing the commit's tree against its parent's tree, and renames are likewise inferred by similarity detection rather than recorded.

All of those objects are immutable and addressed by forty hexadecimal characters nobody wants to type, so refs provide the human-friendly layer. A branch is nothing more than a file under .git/refs/heads whose entire contents are the hash of a commit, so that .git/refs/heads/main might hold a single line and creating a branch costs about forty-one bytes. Committing writes the new commit object, then updates the current branch file to point at it, which is the whole mechanism by which a branch moves forward. Tags live in .git/refs/tags and work the same way, with annotated tags adding a tag object of their own that carries a message and signature, and remote-tracking branches such as origin/main sit under refs/remotes and record where the remote's branches were at your last fetch. The special file .git/HEAD says where you currently are, and normally it contains a symbolic reference like ref: refs/heads/main rather than a hash, so that checking out a branch rewrites that one line; when HEAD instead holds a raw commit hash you are in the detached HEAD state, and new commits will not be reachable from any branch name unless you create one.

Over time Git compacts this structure, since thousands of loose zlib-compressed files are wasteful. Running git gc, or a push or fetch, packs objects into files under objects/pack, where similar objects are stored as deltas against one another, and it collapses many ref files into a single packed-refs file, though the model you reason about stays the same throughout. To see all of it directly, try git cat-file -p HEAD to print your latest commit, then git cat-file -p on the tree hash it shows, and follow the hashes down to a blob; every Git command you use daily is ultimately reading and writing these four kinds of things.
